questions.stem: How many moles are in 4.8 g of magnesium? [Ar: Mg = 24]
questions.explanation: Moles = mass / Ar = 4.8 / 24 = 0.2 moles. Since magnesium is an element, we use the relative atomic mass (Ar) rather than Mr. One mole of Mg weighs 24 g, so 4.8 g is one-fifth of a mole, or 0.2 mol.

questions.stem: What mass of calcium chloride (CaCl₂) contains 0.5 moles? [Ar: Ca = 40, Cl = 35.5]
questions.explanation: First, Mr of CaCl₂ = 40 + (2 x 35.5) = 40 + 71 = 111. Then, mass = moles x Mr = 0.5 x 111 = 55.5 g. Remember that CaCl₂ contains 2 chlorine atoms, so you must multiply the Ar of chlorine by 2.

questions.stem: A student has 3.2 g of sulfur (S) and 3.2 g of oxygen (O₂). Which has more moles? [Ar: S = 32, O = 16]

options.text: They have the same number of moles

questions.explanation: Moles of S = 3.2 / 32 = 0.1 mol. For O₂, Mr = 2 x 16 = 32, so moles of O₂ = 3.2 / 32 = 0.1 mol. They have the same moles of molecules. However, each O₂ molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms, so there are 0.2 mol of oxygen atoms vs 0.1 mol of sulfur atoms. If comparing atoms, oxygen has more. If comparing formula units, they are equal.

questions.stem: Calculate the mass of 2.5 moles of copper sulfate (CuSO₄). [Ar: Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16]
questions.explanation: Mr of CuSO₄ = 64 + 32 + (4 x 16) = 64 + 32 + 64 = 160. Mass = moles x Mr = 2.5 x 160 = 400 g. Always calculate the Mr first, remembering to count all atoms (including the 4 oxygen atoms), then multiply by the number of moles.

questions.stem: A sample of gas has a mass of 8.8 g and contains 0.2 moles. What is the relative formula mass of the gas?
questions.explanation: Rearranging moles = mass / Mr gives Mr = mass / moles = 8.8 / 0.2 = 44. This is the Mr of carbon dioxide (CO₂) = 12 + (2 x 16) = 44. Being able to rearrange the moles equation is an essential skill for GCSE chemistry.
